name: 総代 麺家 あくた川 (Sodai Menya Akutagawa)

claims.text: Iekei ramen here uses wheat noodles boiled in shared water and a soy-sauce (wheat shoyu) tare, so gluten is intrinsic to the dish and unavoidable.
The broth is a pork-bone soy-sauce (豚骨醤油) base typical of iekei, meaning wheat-containing shoyu is in the tare.
Broth is pork-bone and chicken-bone based with pork chashu; no plant-based broth or noodles are available, so the dish is inherently non-vegan.
The ramen is a shoyu (soy sauce) tare style; standard Japanese shoyu is brewed with wheat, so the broth/tare should be assumed to contain wheat.
Broth is a pork stock (豚清湯) and the brand centers on its roast pork (焼き豚); bowls are topped with chashu, so no component is free of animal products.

name: 大豊ラーメン 木屋町店 (Taiho Ramen Kiyamachi)

claims.text: The bowl is built on a pork-bone soy (shoyu) base; standard Japanese soy sauce tare contains wheat, and wheat ramen noodles are cooked in shared water.
Broth is pork-bone/chicken based and bowls are topped with chashu pork; no separate vegan preparation is indicated.

name: 大勝軒 千代原口店 (Taishoken Chiyoharaguchi-ten)

claims.text: Wheat tsukemen/ramen noodles are the core product, prepared in a shared kitchen, so flour cross-contact is unavoidable.
The dipping broth blends chicken, pork and seafood and is sweet-savory, consistent with a wheat-based shoyu tare; no gluten-free tare is indicated.
Broth is animal-based (chicken and pork bones plus seafood) and bowls are topped with pork chashu, menma and narutomaki; no vegan preparation exists here.

name: 台湾まぜそば専門店 脳天喜。 (Taiwan Mazesoba Senmonten Noutenki (Kyoto Me)

claims.text: The kitchen is built around wheat noodles and a soy-sauce-based Taiwanese mince; no gluten-free handling or separate prep is described, so heavy gluten cross-contact should be assumed.
Taiwanese mazesoba tare is conventionally a wheat-based soy-sauce mince; no wheat-free tamari is mentioned.
Menu is pork- and egg-forward (dongpo pork, pork mince, chashu, 味玉); no vegan bowl, and shared equipment with meat dishes should be assumed.
Wheat ramen noodles are cooked in shared boiling water on a single ramen line, so any bowl carries gluten and cross-contact risk; no gluten-free preparation is mentioned anywhere.
The shop is a Kyoto soy-sauce (shoyu) ramen specialist; the tare is a standard soy-based seasoning, which in this style is wheat-containing soy sauce, with no gluten-free alternative noted.

Every bowl is built on a multi-hour pork-bone and chicken-bone broth finished with pork back-fat and topped with pork chashu, so the cooking line is fundamentally animal-based with no separate vegan preparation.
The signature chili topping can be omitted on request, since it is sprinkled on top rather than cooked into the broth.

name: 天下一品 総本店 (Tenkaippin Sohonten)

claims.text: Wheat ramen noodles and wheat-based shoyu tare are core to every bowl; the same kitchen also handles gyoza, karaage and fried rice, so cross-contact with gluten is unavoidable.
The standard ramen tare is soy-sauce based, which in Japan is normally brewed with wheat; no wheat-free tare is offered.
The base broth is simmered from chicken bones; flagship specials use beef tendon and pork, so no preparation surface or stock is free of animal products.

name: 特製ラーメン 大中 本店 (Tokusei Ramen Daichu Honten)

claims.text: Core dish is wheat ramen noodles in a pork/chicken broth with a soy-sauce (shoyu) tare; gyoza (wheat) and garlic chips are on the menu. No gluten-free option or allergen handling indicated.
The signature broth is 濃厚豚骨醤油 (rich pork-bone soy sauce), meaning a wheat-based soy tare is integral to the bowl.
Broth is made by simmering pork bones and chicken bones for 24 hours; there is no plant-based broth or vegan bowl available.
